arXiv:1806.07022v1 [math.NT] 19 Jun 2018

On some generalizations of the sum of powers of natural numbers

Andrei K. Svinin Address: Andrei K. Svinin, Matrosov Institute for System Dynamics and Control Theory of Siberian Branch of Russian Academy of Sciences, P.O. Box 292, 664033 Irkutsk, Russia Email address: svinin@icc.ru
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this paper some generalizations of the sum of powers of natural numbers is considered. In particular, the class of sums whose generating function is the power of the generating function for the classical sums of powers is studying. The so-called binomial sums are also considered. The problem of constructing polynomials that allow to calculate the values of the corresponding sums in certain cases is solved.

1. Introduction

Power-sum

Sm​(n):=∑q=1nqm,m≥0S_{m}(n):=\sum_{q=1}^{n}q^{m},\;\;m\geq 0 (1.1)

starting with the works of Blaise Pascal, Johann Faulhaber, Jacob Bernoulli for centuries, has been the object of active research. The expression (1.1) defines a function on the set of natural numbers. Pascal’s theorem asserts that for any integer degree m≥0m\geq 0, the value of the sum (1.1) can be obtained as the value of the corresponding polynomial S^m​(n)\hat{S}_{m}(n). The exponential generating function (e.g.f.) for sums of the form (1.1) is given by

G⁡(n,t)\displaystyle G(n,t) =\displaystyle= ∑j≥0Sj​(n)​tjj!=∑j≥0(∑q=1nqj​tjj!)=∑q=1neq​t\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq 0}S_{j}(n)\frac{t^{j}}{j!}=\sum_{j\geq 0}\left(\sum_{q=1}^{n}q^{j}\frac{t^{j}}{j!}\right)=\sum_{q=1}^{n}e^{qt} (1.2)
=\displaystyle= e(n+1)​t−etet−1.\displaystyle\frac{e^{(n+1)t}-e^{t}}{e^{t}-1}.

In turn, the expansion (1.2) into an infinite series

G⁡(n,t)=∑q≥0S^q​(n)​tqq!G(n,t)=\sum_{q\geq 0}\hat{S}_{q}(n)\frac{t^{q}}{q!}

gives an infinite set of polynomials {S^m​(n):m≥0}\{\hat{S}_{m}(n):m\geq 0\} whose values for natural nn give the values of the corresponding sums. In 1713, Jacob Bernoulli published an expression for the sum of the degree mm of the first nn natural numbers as a polynomial of (m+1)(m+1)-th degree in nn, which is determined by some infinite set of rational numbers {Bm:m≥0}\{B_{m}:m\geq 0\}, which are now called the Bernoulli numbers.

We will write this expression in the following form:

S^m​(n)=1m+1​∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+1q)​Bq​nm+1−q.\hat{S}_{m}(n)=\frac{1}{m+1}\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+1\choose q}B_{q}n^{m+1-q}. (1.3)

Faulhaber’s theorem, in turn, asserts that, for odd values of mm, the polynomial (1.3) is actually a polynomial in w:=n⁡(n+1)w:=n(n+1). To a certain extent this is due to the fact that all odd Bernoulli numbers starting with the third one are zero [15]. In turn, it is known that for any mm, any polynomial (1.3) can be written as some polynomial in ww multiplied by 2​n+12n+1 [12].

In applications there can arise not only sums of the form (1.1), but also other sums involving the powers of natural numbers. For example, Johann Faulhaber considered the so-called kk-fold sums Smk​(n)S^{k}_{m}(n) defined by the recurrence relation

Smk​(n)=∑q=1nSmk−1​(q),∀k≥1S^{k}_{m}(n)=\sum_{q=1}^{n}S^{k-1}_{m}(q),\;\;\forall k\geq 1

starting from Sm0​(n):=nmS^{0}_{m}(n):=n^{m}. When considering such generalizations, the question always arises about of polynomials that, like (1.3), help to calculate the values of corresponding sums.

In this paper we consider some generalizations of power-sum (1.1) and set the problem of finding the corresponding polynomials. In the next section, we define a some class of sums whose e.g.f. is the kk-th power of the generating function (1.2), with kk being an arbitrary natural number. We denote these sums by the symbol Sm(k)​(n)S^{(k)}_{m}(n) and call them power-sums of higher order. One of our results is that we found an expression for the associated polynomials similar to the formula (1.3). These polynomials, in contrast to (1.3), are determined by higher-order Bernoulli numbers. This is, although not obvious, is quite natural. In the next section we give some information about higher-order Bernoulli numbers and about the Stirling numbers of the second kind, which are also involved in the formula for these polynomials. In the second section, we also investigate some rational roots of polynomials corresponding to higher order power-sums. In the third section, we discuss some generalizations of the sums (1.1) arising in applications, namely, a some class of multiple sums.

2. higher order power-sums

2.1. Definition of higher order power-sums

Let us consider the power of the e.g.f. (1.2):

(G⁡(n,t))k:=∑q≥0Sq(k)​(n)​tqq!.\left(G(n,t)\right)^{k}:=\sum_{q\geq 0}S_{q}^{(k)}(n)\frac{t^{q}}{q!}.

We have

(G⁡(n,t))k=(∑q=1neq​t)k=∑q=0k⁡(n−1)(kq)n​e(k+q)​t,\left(G(n,t)\right)^{k}=\left(\sum_{q=1}^{n}e^{qt}\right)^{k}=\sum_{q=0}^{k(n-1)}{k\choose q}_{n}e^{(k+q)t}, (2.1)

where the symbol (kq)n{k\choose q}_{n} stands for polynomial coefficients defined through the relation

(∑q=1ntq)k:=∑q=0k⁡(n−1)(kq)n​tk+q.\left(\sum_{q=1}^{n}t^{q}\right)^{k}:=\sum_{q=0}^{k(n-1)}{k\choose q}_{n}t^{k+q}.

It should be noted that the coefficients (kq)n{k\choose q}_{n}, naturally generalizing the binomial coefficients (n=2n=2), originated from Abraham De Moivre and Leonhard Euler works [16], [7]. Then they were rediscovered in the works [17] and [23] and later were studied in detail in the literature due to their good applicability. By direct computation we derive

Proposition 2.1.

The expression (2.1) is the e.g.f. for sums of the form

Sm(k)​(n)=∑q=0k⁡(n−1)(kq)n​(k+q)m.S_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\sum_{q=0}^{k(n-1)}{k\choose q}_{n}\left(k+q\right)^{m}. (2.2)

It is evident, that these sums, by definition, are the result of successive binomial convolutions, that is,

Sm(k)​(n)=∑q=0m(mq)​Sq(k−1)​(n)​Sm−q​(n),k≥2.S_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m\choose q}S_{q}^{(k-1)}(n)S_{m-q}(n),\;\;k\geq 2.

It is also obvious that this is true for the corresponding polynomials S^m(k)​(n)\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n). The following property holds:

Proposition 2.2.

The sums Sm(k)​(n)S_{m}^{(k)}(n) satisfy the recurrence relation

∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+kq)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Sq(r)​(n)\displaystyle\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+k\choose q}S(m+k-q,k)S_{q}^{(r)}(n)
=1(kr)​∑j=0m(−1)j​(m+km+k−r−j)​S​(m+k−r−j,k−r)​S​(r+j,r)​nr+j.\displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;=\frac{1}{{k\choose r}}\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^{j}{m+k\choose m+k-r-j}S(m+k-r-j,k-r)S(r+j,r)n^{r+j}. (2.3)

where S⁡(n,k)S(n,k) are the Stirling numbers of the second kind.

Proof.

The proposition is proved with the help of standard arguments. Let us make the change of the argument of the e.g.f. (1.2): t→−tt\rightarrow-t. Obviously, the following relation holds

(−1)r​(e−n​t−1et−1)r=∑q≥0(−1)q​Sq(r)​(n)​tqq!.(-1)^{r}\left(\frac{e^{-nt}-1}{e^{t}-1}\right)^{r}=\sum_{q\geq 0}(-1)^{q}S^{(r)}_{q}(n)\frac{t^{q}}{q!}. (2.4)

Multiplying both sides of (2.4) by (et−1)k(e^{t}-1)^{k} and taking into account that

(et−1)k=k!​(∑q≥0S⁡(q,k)​tqq!),∀k≥0,(e^{t}-1)^{k}=k!\left(\sum_{q\geq 0}S(q,k)\frac{t^{q}}{q!}\right),\;\;\forall k\geq 0,

we obtain, as a result, the relation (2.3). ∎

As a special case of (2.3), for r=kr=k, we get

∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+kq)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Sq(k)​(n)=(−1)m​S​(k+m,k)​nm+k.\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+k\choose q}S(m+k-q,k)S_{q}^{(k)}(n)=(-1)^{m}S(k+m,k)n^{m+k}.

In turn, if k=1k=1, then the last relation turns into a well-known relation for the classical sums of powers [19]. The following theorem gives a some representation of the polynomials S^m(k)​(n)\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n).

Theorem 2.3.

The polynomials S^m(k)​(n)\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n) can be written as

S^m(k)​(n)=1(m+kk)​∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+kq)​Bq(k)​S​(m+k−q,k)​nm+k−q,\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\frac{1}{{m+k\choose k}}\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+k\choose q}B_{q}^{(k)}S(m+k-q,k)n^{m+k-q}, (2.5)

where Bq(k)B_{q}^{(k)} are the Bernoulli numbers of higher order that are defined by the e.g.f.

tk(et−1)k=∑q≥0Bq(k)​tqq!.\frac{t^{k}}{(e^{t}-1)^{k}}=\sum_{q\geq 0}B^{(k)}_{q}\frac{t^{q}}{q!}. (2.6)

Comparing (2.5) with the formula (1.3), we see that the Bernoulli numbers here are replaced by their higher analogs. Moreover we see that this expression, in contrast with (1.3), involves the Stirling numbers of the second kind.

2.2. Bernoulli numbers of higher order

The classical Bernoulli numbers are known to be uniquely determined by the e.g.f. [11]

tet−1=∑q≥0Bq​tqq!.\frac{t}{e^{t}-1}=\sum_{q\geq 0}B_{q}\frac{t^{q}}{q!}. (2.7)

It follows from (2.7) the recurrence relation

∑q=0m(m+1q)​Bq=δ0,m.\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m+1\choose q}B_{q}=\delta_{0,m}. (2.8)

This relation, in fact, is one of the many recurrence relations for the Bernoulli numbers (see, for example, [2]). For example, one can derive a countable set of recurrence relations of the form

∑q=0m(m+kq)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Bq=m+kk​S​(m+k−1,k−1),∀k≥1.\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m+k\choose q}S(m+k-q,k)B_{q}=\frac{m+k}{k}S(m+k-1,k-1),\;\;\forall k\geq 1. (2.9)

The numbers Bn(k)B_{n}^{(k)} first appeared in the work of Nörlund [18] in connection with the theory of finite differences and were subsequently investigated from various points of view (see, for example, [3]). It is known that they are related to each other by the recurrence relation [18]

Bn(k+1)=k−nk​Bn(k)−n​Bn−1(k).B_{n}^{(k+1)}=\frac{k-n}{k}B_{n}^{(k)}-nB_{n-1}^{(k)}. (2.10)

It should be noted that Bn(k)B^{(k)}_{n} for some fixed n≥0n\geq 0 is calculated as the value of some polynomial in kk. In what follows we shall use for these polynomials the same notation Bn(k)B^{(k)}_{n} in the hope that this will not lead to confusion. In the literature, polynomials of this type are called the Nörlund polynomials. The first six of them are as follows

B0(k)=1,B1(k)=−12​k,B2(k)=112​k​(3​k−1),B3(k)=−18​k2​(k−1),B_{0}^{(k)}=1,\;\;B_{1}^{(k)}=-\frac{1}{2}k,\;\;B_{2}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{12}k\left(3k-1\right),\;\;B_{3}^{(k)}=-\frac{1}{8}k^{2}\left(k-1\right),
B4(k)=k240​(15​k3−30​k2+5​k+2),B5(k)=−196​k2​(k−1)​(3​k2−7​k−2).B_{4}^{(k)}=\frac{k}{240}\left(15k^{3}-30k^{2}+5k+2\right),\;\;B_{5}^{(k)}=-\frac{1}{96}k^{2}\left(k-1\right)\left(3k^{2}-7k-2\right).
Remark 2.4.

By standard arguments, using the e.g.f. (2.6), we can derive the following recurrence relation:

∑q=0m(m+kq)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Bq(r)=(m+kk)(m+k−rk−r)​S​(m+k−r,k−r),∀k≥r,\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m+k\choose q}S(m+k-q,k)B_{q}^{(r)}=\frac{{m+k\choose k}}{{m+k-r\choose k-r}}S(m+k-r,k-r),\;\;\forall k\geq r, (2.11)

the particular case of which is (2.9). Making use (2.11), we can prove that polynomials defined by the formula (2.5) satisfy the recurrence relation (2.3), but this is not necessary here.

2.3. Stirling numbers of the second kind

The numbers S⁡(n,k)S(n,k) in the formula (2.5), as mentioned above, are Stirling numbers of the second kind. As is known, they satisfy the identity

S⁡(n,k)=S⁡(n−1,k−1)+k​S​(n−1,k)S(n,k)=S(n-1,k-1)+kS(n-1,k) (2.12)

and some boundary conditions [11]. The Stirling numbers S⁡(m+k,k)S(m+k,k) for some fixed m≥0m\geq 0 can be calculated as the values of some polynomial fm​(k)f_{m}(k) of degree 2​m2m. These polynomials satisfy the recurrence identity

fm​(k)−fm​(k−1)=k​fm−1​(k),f_{m}(k)-f_{m}(k-1)=kf_{m-1}(k), (2.13)

which easily follows from the identity (2.12). In the literature they are known as the Stirling polynomials [9], [10], [13]. The comparison (2.10) and (2.13) shows that the Nörlund and Stirling polynomials are related by the relation (see, for example, [1])

fm​(k)=(m+km)​Bm(−k).f_{m}(k)={m+k\choose m}B_{m}^{(-k)}. (2.14)

Using (2.14), we can rewrite (2.11) in the form

∑q=0m(mq)​Bm−q(−k)​Bq(r)=Bm(r−k).\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m\choose q}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}B_{q}^{(r)}=B_{m}^{(r-k)}.

The last relation is completely obvious, since it is simply a overwriting of the relation Br−k=Br​B−kB^{r-k}=B^{r}B^{-k}, where B=B⁡(t)B=B(t) is the e.g.f. of the Bernoulli numbers.

2.4. Proof of the theorem 2.3

In the formula (2.5) we can replace S⁡(m+k−q,k)S(m+k-q,k) by fm−q​(k)f_{m-q}(k) and get the following representation:

S^m(k)​(n)=1(m+kk)​∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+kq)​(m−q+km−q)​Bq(k)​Bm−q(−k)​nm−q+k.\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\frac{1}{{m+k\choose k}}\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+k\choose q}{m-q+k\choose m-q}B_{q}^{(k)}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}n^{m-q+k}. (2.15)

In turn, using the binomial identity

(m+kq)​(m−q+km−q)=(m+kk)​(mq),{m+k\choose q}{m-q+k\choose m-q}={m+k\choose k}{m\choose q},

we obtain a simpler expression

S^m(k)​(n)=nk​∑q=0m(−1)q​(mq)​Bq(k)​Bm−q(−k)​nm−q.\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n)=n^{k}\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m\choose q}B_{q}^{(k)}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}n^{m-q}. (2.16)

The formula (2.16) represents the binomial convolution of two sequences: {am:=(−1)mBm(k)}\{a_{m}:=(-1)^{m}B_{m}^{(k)}\} and {bm:=Bm(−k)nm+k}\{b_{m}:=B_{m}^{(-k)}n^{m+k}\}. In turn, the e.g.f.’s of these sequences, as can be easily verified, are the kk-degree of two e.g.f.’s

A⁡(t)=−te−t−1​and​C​(n,t)=en​t−1t.A(t)=\frac{-t}{e^{-t}-1}\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;C(n,t)=\frac{e^{nt}-1}{t}. (2.17)

It is obvious that the representation of the e.g.f. (1.2) in the factorized form G⁡(n,t)=A⁡(t)​C​(n,t)G(n,t)=A(t)C(n,t) gives the simplest way to express the polynomials S^m​(n)\hat{S}_{m}(n) in terms of Bernoulli numbers. Since the expression (2.16) is equivalent (2.15), the theorem 2.3 should be considered proven.

2.5. Some properties of the polynomials S^m(k)​(n)\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n)

In what follows we will consider these polynomials in the continuous variable z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}, so that we can talk about their derivatives. It is more convenient to investigate the polynomials11 1 Obviously, S^m(k)​(z)=zk​Qm(k)​(z)\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(z)=z^{k}Q_{m}^{(k)}(z).

Qm(k)​(z)=∑q=0m(−1)q​(mq)​Bq(k)​Bm−q(−k)​zm−q.Q_{m}^{(k)}(z)=\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m\choose q}B_{q}^{(k)}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}z^{m-q}.

The following lemma will be useful for what follows.

Lemma 2.5.

The following two identities are valid:

∑q=0m−1(mq)⁡(m−q)​Bq(k)​Bm−q(−k)={−k​B1,m=1,k​Bm,∀m≥2\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}{m\choose q}(m-q)B_{q}^{(k)}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}-kB_{1},\;\;m=1,\\[5.69046pt] kB_{m},\;\;\forall m\geq 2\end{array}\right. (2.18)

and

∑q=0m−2(mq)⁡(m−q)​(m−q−1)​Bq(k)​Bm−q(−k)={−k⁡(3​k−1)​B2−2​k2​B1,m=2,−k⁡((m+1)​k−m+1)​Bm+m​k2​Bm−1,∀m≥3.\sum_{q=0}^{m-2}{m\choose q}(m-q)(m-q-1)B_{q}^{(k)}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}-k(3k-1)B_{2}-2k^{2}B_{1},\;\;m=2,\\[5.69046pt] -k((m+1)k-m+1)B_{m}+mk^{2}B_{m-1},\;\;\forall m\geq 3.\end{array}\right. (2.19)
Proof.

Let B(k)=B(k)​(t)B^{(k)}=B^{(k)}(t) be the e.g.f. of the Bernoulli numbers of higher order (2.6). We have

t​d​B(−k)d​t​B(k)=k​t​etet−1−k=k⁡(A−1),t\frac{dB^{(-k)}}{dt}B^{(k)}=kt\frac{e^{t}}{e^{t}-1}-k=k\left(A-1\right),

where A=A⁡(t)A=A(t) is supposed to be the e.g.f. defined in (2.17). This relation implies (2.18). To show (2.19), one needs to calculate

t2​d2​B(−k)d​t2​B(k)\displaystyle t^{2}\frac{d^{2}B^{(-k)}}{dt^{2}}B^{(k)} =\displaystyle= t2​(k2−k)​e2​t(et−1)2+(t−2​k)​k​t​etet−1+k2+k\displaystyle\frac{t^{2}(k^{2}-k)e^{2t}}{(e^{t}-1)^{2}}+\frac{(t-2k)kte^{t}}{e^{t}-1}+k^{2}+k (2.20)
=\displaystyle= k2​(A−1)2−k⁡(A2−t​A−1).\displaystyle k^{2}\left(A-1\right)^{2}-k\left(A^{2}-tA-1\right).

Taking into account the recurrence relation (2.10), we derive from (2.20) the relation (2.19). ∎

Remark 2.6.

We could write (2.18) as

∑q=0m−1(mq)⁡(m−q)​Bq(k)​Bm−q(−k)=(−1)m​k​Bm,∀m≥1.\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}{m\choose q}(m-q)B_{q}^{(k)}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}=(-1)^{m}kB_{m},\;\;\forall m\geq 1.

However, considering the fact that the Bernoulli numbers are nonzero only for even mm and m=1m=1, we can get rid of the minus sign. A similar remark applies to the formula (2.19).

Now we in a position to formulate some statements about the rational zeros of the polynomials Qm(k)​(z)Q_{m}^{(k)}(z).

Theorem 2.7.

The following two statements are true:

  • 1)

    The polynomial Qm(k)​(z)Q_{m}^{(k)}(z) has a simple root z0=−1z_{0}=-1 for even mm and m=1m=1 and any k≥1k\geq 1;

  • 2)

    The polynomial Qm(k)​(z)Q_{m}^{(k)}(z) has a double root z0=−1z_{0}=-1 for odd m≥3m\geq 3 and any k≥1k\geq 1.

Proof.

It is obvious that

Qm(k)​(−1)=(−1)m​∑q=0m(mq)​Bq(k)​Bm−q(−k)=0,∀m≥1,Q_{m}^{(k)}(-1)=(-1)^{m}\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m\choose q}B_{q}^{(k)}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}=0,\;\;\forall m\geq 1,

i.e, for any m≥1m\geq 1 and k≥1k\geq 1, the polynomial Qm(k)​(z)Q_{m}^{(k)}(z) has the root z0=−1z_{0}=-1. Further, we have

d​Qm(k)​(z)d​z|=z=−1(−1)m−1∑q=0m−1(mq)(m−q)Bq(k)Bm−q(−k)\frac{dQ_{m}^{(k)}(z)}{dz}\left|{}_{z=-1}\right.=(-1)^{m-1}\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}{m\choose q}(m-q)B_{q}^{(k)}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}

and by (2.18), we obtain

d​Qm(k)​(z)d​z|z=−1=−kBm,\frac{dQ_{m}^{(k)}(z)}{dz}\left|{}_{z=-1}\right.=-kB_{m},

We know that the Bernoulli numbers BmB_{m} are nonzero for even mm and m=1m=1. Thus, the first part of the sentence (2.7) is proved. For odd m≥3m\geq 3, the Bernoulli numbers are equal zero and therefore the multiplicity of the root z0=−1z_{0}=-1 is at least equal to two. Next, we calculate

d2​Qm(k)​(z)d​z2|=z=−1(−1)m∑q=0m−2(mq)(m−q)(m−q−1)Bq(k)Bm−q(−k).\frac{d^{2}Q_{m}^{(k)}(z)}{dz^{2}}\left|{}_{z=-1}\right.=(-1)^{m}\sum_{q=0}^{m-2}{m\choose q}(m-q)(m-q-1)B_{q}^{(k)}B_{m-q}^{(-k)}.

Now we need to use the identity (2.19). By virtue of this identity, the second derivative Qm(k)​(z)Q_{m}^{(k)}(z) at z=−1z=-1 for any m≥2m\geq 2 and k≥1k\geq 1 is not zero. Thus the theorem is proved. ∎

Remark 2.8.

It was shown in the paper [14] that the rational zeros of the polynomials S^m(1)​(z)\hat{S}_{m}^{(1)}(z) are only 0,−10,-1, and −1/2-1/2, and the last value is a simple root for these polynomials with even numbers.

The polynomials Q2(k)​(z)Q_{2}^{(k)}(z) and Q3(k)​(z)Q_{3}^{(k)}(z), as is easily seen, have the following form:

Q2(k)​(z)=k12​(z+1)​((3​k+1)​z+3​k−1)​and​Q3(k)​(z)=k28​(z+1)2​((k+1)​z+k−1).Q_{2}^{(k)}(z)=\frac{k}{12}(z+1)\left((3k+1)z+3k-1\right)\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;Q_{3}^{(k)}(z)=\frac{k^{2}}{8}(z+1)^{2}\left((k+1)z+k-1\right).

Hence it is obvious that

Q2(k)​(−3​k−13​k+1)=0,∀k≥1​and​Q3(k)​(−k−1k+1)=0,∀k≥2.Q_{2}^{(k)}\left(-\frac{3k-1}{3k+1}\right)=0,\;\;\forall k\geq 1\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;Q_{3}^{(k)}\left(-\frac{k-1}{k+1}\right)=0,\;\;\forall k\geq 2.

3. Other generalizations of power-sums

3.1. Multiple sums

In the paper [22], we considered multiple sums of the form

𝒮~m(k)​(n):=∑{q}∈Bk,k​n(q1m+(q2−n)m+⋯+(qk−k​n+n)m),\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_{m}^{(k)}(n):=\sum_{\{q\}\in B_{k,kn}}\left(q_{1}^{m}+(q_{2}-n)^{m}+\cdots+(q_{k}-kn+n)^{m}\right), (3.1)

where the exponent mm is supposed to be odd. Here Bk,s:={qj:1≤q1≤⋯≤qk≤s}B_{k,s}:=\{q_{j}:1\leq q_{1}\leq\cdots\leq q_{k}\leq s\}. Obviously, if mm is odd, then the value of qmq^{m} with negative qq in (3.1) is qm=−|q|mq^{m}=-|q|^{m}. According to this rule, a sum of the form (3.1) can be rewritten as

𝒮~m(k)​(n)=∑q=1k​ncq​(k,n)​qm\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\sum_{q=1}^{kn}c_{q}(k,n)q^{m} (3.2)

with some integer coefficients cq​(k,n)c_{q}(k,n).

Example 3.1.

In the case k=2k=2, we have

𝒮~m(2)​(n)\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_{m}^{(2)}(n) =\displaystyle= ∑{q}∈B2,2​n(q1m+(q2−n)m)\displaystyle\sum_{\{q\}\in B_{2,2n}}\left(q_{1}^{m}+(q_{2}-n)^{m}\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑j=1n−1(∑q=1jqm−j​(n−j)m)+∑j=1n(∑q=1n+jqm+(n+j)​jm).\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\left(\sum_{q=1}^{j}q^{m}-j(n-j)^{m}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{q=1}^{n+j}q^{m}+(n+j)j^{m}\right).

Hence we get

cq​(2,n)={2​n+q+1,  1≤q≤n,2​n−q+1,n+1≤q≤2​n.c_{q}(2,n)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}2n+q+1,\;\;1\leq q\leq n,\\[5.69046pt] 2n-q+1,\;\;n+1\leq q\leq 2n.\end{array}\right.

At first glance, multiple sums (3.1) have nothing to do with higher order power-sums (2.2). However, in the paper [22], it was conjectured that, in the case of odd mm, the sum 𝒮~m(k)​(n)\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_{m}^{(k)}(n) can be expressed as22 2 In this paper, the sums Sm(k)​(n)S_{m}^{(k)}(n) were not identified as sums of higher orders.

𝒮~m(k)​(n)=∑q=0k−1(k⁡(n+1)q)​Sm(k−q)​(n).\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\sum_{q=0}^{k-1}{k(n+1)\choose q}S_{m}^{(k-q)}(n). (3.3)

This hypothesis was based on numerous calculations using computer algebra method. Note that for k=1k=1 the hypothesis is clear, and for k=2k=2 it is easy to prove. By the way, if (3.3) is true, then it follows that the integer coefficients cq​(k,n)c_{q}(k,n) are, in addition, non-zero and positive.

3.2. Binomial sums

On the right-hand side of (3.3) there is a sum, which we, somewhat conditionally, call binomial. Let us, throughout the rest of the paper, study a sum of the form [22]

𝒮m(k)​(n)=∑q=0k−1(k⁡(n+1)q)​Sm(k−q)​(n).\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\sum_{q=0}^{k-1}{k(n+1)\choose q}S_{m}^{(k-q)}(n). (3.4)

In what follows, it is useful to consider its particular case

𝒮m(k)​(1)=∑q=0k−1(2​kq)​(k−q)m.\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(1)=\sum_{q=0}^{k-1}{2k\choose q}(k-q)^{m}.

Observe that in the case of an odd exponent mm, we can write

2​𝒮m(k)​(1)=∑q=02​k(2​kq)​|k−q|m.2\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(1)=\sum_{q=0}^{2k}{2k\choose q}|k-q|^{m}. (3.5)

On the right-hand side of this identity there is the binomial sum which was investigated in the papers [21], [24]. Using the relation (3.5), we can transfer some results of [24] to the sum 𝒮m(k)​(1)\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(1).

Proposition 3.2.

The sum 𝒮m(k)​(1)\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(1) satisfies the recurrence relation

𝒮m+2(k)​(1)=k2​𝒮m(k)​(1)−2​k​(2​k−1)​𝒮m(k−1)​(1).\mathcal{S}_{m+2}^{(k)}(1)=k^{2}\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(1)-2k(2k-1)\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k-1)}(1). (3.6)
Proof.

We have

k2​𝒮m(k)​(1)−𝒮m+2(k)​(1)\displaystyle k^{2}\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(1)-\mathcal{S}_{m+2}^{(k)}(1) =\displaystyle= ∑q=1k−1(2​kq)​(k−q)m​(k2−(k−q)2)\displaystyle\sum_{q=1}^{k-1}{2k\choose q}(k-q)^{m}\left(k^{2}-(k-q)^{2}\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑q=1k−1(2​kq)​(k−q)m​q​(2​k−q).\displaystyle\sum_{q=1}^{k-1}{2k\choose q}(k-q)^{m}q\left(2k-q\right).

Using the binomial identity

(2​kq)=(2​k−2q−1)​2​k​(2​k−1)q⁡(2​k−q),{2k\choose q}={2k-2\choose q-1}\frac{2k(2k-1)}{q(2k-q)},

we obtain, as a result, the relation (3.6). ∎

Proposition 3.3.

There is an infinite set of polynomials {Pm​(k):m≥0}\{P_{m}(k):m\geq 0\} such that,

𝒮2​r+1(k)​(1)=Pr​(k)​k2​(2​kk).\mathcal{S}_{2r+1}^{(k)}(1)=P_{r}(k)\frac{k}{2}{2k\choose k}. (3.7)
Proof.

Let us first calculate 𝒮1(k)​(1)\mathcal{S}_{1}^{(k)}(1). We have

𝒮1(k)​(1)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{1}^{(k)}(1) =\displaystyle= ∑q=0k(2​kq)⁡(k−q)=12​∑q=0k(2​kq)⁡((2​k−q)−q)\displaystyle\sum_{q=0}^{k}{2k\choose q}(k-q)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{q=0}^{k}{2k\choose q}\left((2k-q)-q\right)
=\displaystyle= 12​∑q=0k(2​kq)⁡(2​k−q)−12​∑q=1k(2​kq)​q.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{q=0}^{k}{2k\choose q}(2k-q)-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{q=1}^{k}{2k\choose q}q.

Using binomial identities

(2​kq)=2​k2​k−q​(2​k−1q)=2​kq​(2​k−1q−1),{2k\choose q}=\frac{2k}{2k-q}{2k-1\choose q}=\frac{2k}{q}{2k-1\choose q-1},

we get

𝒮1(k)​(1)=k​∑q=0k(2​k−1q)−k​∑q=1k(2​k−1q−1)=k​(2​k−1k)=k2​(2​kk).\mathcal{S}_{1}^{(k)}(1)=k\sum_{q=0}^{k}{2k-1\choose q}-k\sum_{q=1}^{k}{2k-1\choose q-1}=k{2k-1\choose k}=\frac{k}{2}{2k\choose k}.

Thus, 𝒮1(k)​(1)\mathcal{S}_{1}^{(k)}(1) is actually calculated by the formula (3.7), with P0​(k)=1P_{0}(k)=1. Now, using the identity (3.6) and the binomial identity

2​k​(2​k−1)​(2​k−2k−1)=k2​(2​kk),2k(2k-1){2k-2\choose k-1}=k^{2}{2k\choose k},

we see that if 𝒮2​r+1(k)​(1)\mathcal{S}_{2r+1}^{(k)}(1) is expressed by the formula (3.7) with some polynomial Pr​(k)P_{r}(k), then 𝒮2​r+3(k)​(1)\mathcal{S}_{2r+3}^{(k)}(1) is also expressed by this expression with some polynomial Pr+1​(k)P_{r+1}(k), defined by

Pr+1​(k)=k2​Pr​(k)−k⁡(k−1)​Pr​(k−1).P_{r+1}(k)=k^{2}P_{r}(k)-k(k-1)P_{r}(k-1). (3.8)

Therefore, by the method of mathematical induction, we prove the proposition. ∎

It is important to observe that the polynomials Pr​(k)P_{r}(k) are closely related to the well-known Gandhi polynomials [8], that are defined by the recurrence relation

Fr+1​(k)=(k+1)2​Fr​(k+1)−k2​Fr​(k),F_{r+1}(k)=(k+1)^{2}F_{r}(k+1)-k^{2}F_{r}(k),

starting with F1​(k)=1F_{1}(k)=1. Indeed, it is not hard to see that Pr​(k)=(−1)r+1​k​Fr​(−k)P_{r}(k)=(-1)^{r+1}kF_{r}(-k) for r≥1r\geq 1. The first six Gandhi polynomials are as follows:

F1​(k)=1,F2​(k)=2​k+1,F3​(k)=6​k2+8​k+3,F4​(k)=24​k3+60​k2+54​k+17,F_{1}(k)=1,\;\;F_{2}(k)=2k+1,\;\;F_{3}(k)=6k^{2}+8k+3,\;\;F_{4}(k)=24k^{3}+60k^{2}+54k+17,
F5​(k)=120​k4+480​k3+762​k2+556​k+155,F_{5}(k)=120k^{4}+480k^{3}+762k^{2}+556k+155,
F6​(k)=720​k5+4200​k4+10248​k3+12840​k2+8146​k+2073.F_{6}(k)=720k^{5}+4200k^{4}+10248k^{3}+12840k^{2}+8146k+2073.
Remark 3.4.

The Gandhi polynomials appeared in the paper [8], in which the hypothesis was formulated that Fr​(0)=|G2​r|F_{r}(0)=|G_{2r}|, where G2​r=2​(1−4r)​B2​rG_{2r}=2(1-4^{r})B_{2r} are the alternating Genocci numbers determined by the e.g.f.

2​tet+1=t+∑q≥1G2​q​t2​q(2​q)!.\frac{2t}{e^{t}+1}=t+\sum_{q\geq 1}G_{2q}\frac{t^{2q}}{(2q)!}.

This hypothesis was proved in the papers [4], [20]. It should be noted that the Genocci numbers, unlike the Bernoulli numbers, are integers.

Remark 3.5.

The Gandhi polynomials can be written as Fr​(k)=Fr​(1,1,k)F_{r}(k)=F_{r}(1,1,k), where Fr​(x,y,z)F_{r}(x,y,z) are some polynomials of three variables that are defined by the recurrence relation

Fr+1​(x,y,z)=(z+x)​(z+y)​Fr​(x,y,z+1)−z2​Fr​(x,y,z),F_{r+1}(x,y,z)=(z+x)(z+y)F_{r}(x,y,z+1)-z^{2}F_{r}(x,y,z),

starting with F1​(x,y,z)=1F_{1}(x,y,z)=1. In the literature, these polynomials are known as the Dumont-Foath polynomials [5], [6]. It turns out that these polynomials are symmetric with respect to the variables x,y,zx,y,z. The main property of these polynomials is that Fr​(1,1,1)=|G2​r+2|F_{r}(1,1,1)=|G_{2r+2}|.

We observe now that the formula (3.7) can be rewritten in the form

𝒮2​r+1(k)​(1)=(−1)r+1​Fr​(−k)​k2​(2​k−1k−1)\mathcal{S}_{2r+1}^{(k)}(1)=(-1)^{r+1}F_{r}(-k)k^{2}{2k-1\choose k-1}

for r≥1r\geq 1.

3.3. Polynomials corresponding to binomial sums

Let us define the set of polynomials {𝒮^m(k)​(z):m≥1}\{\hat{\mathcal{S}}_{m}^{(k)}(z):m\geq 1\} by the relation

𝒮^m(k)​(z)=∑q=0k−1(k⁡(z+1)q)​S^m(k−q)​(z).\hat{\mathcal{S}}_{m}^{(k)}(z)=\sum_{q=0}^{k-1}{k(z+1)\choose q}\hat{S}_{m}^{(k-q)}(z).

Our goal is to describe these polynomials. For the degree m=1m=1 we can formulate the following result:

Proposition 3.6.

The polynomial 𝒮^1(k)​(z)\hat{\mathcal{S}}_{1}^{(k)}(z) can be defined by

𝒮^1(k)​(z)=z⁡(z+1)2​k​(k⁡(z+1)−1k−1),∀k≥1.\hat{\mathcal{S}}_{1}^{(k)}(z)=\frac{z(z+1)}{2}k{k(z+1)-1\choose k-1},\;\;\forall k\geq 1.

To prove this proposition, it suffices to use the following lemma:

Lemma 3.7.

The relation

(k⁡(z+1)−1k−1)=1k​∑q=0k−1(k−q)​(k⁡(z+1)q)​zk−q−1{k(z+1)-1\choose k-1}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{q=0}^{k-1}(k-q){k(z+1)\choose q}z^{k-q-1} (3.9)

is an identity.

Proof.

Let us denote

gk​(z):=k​(k⁡(z+1)−1k−1)​and​g~k​(z):=∑q=0k−1(k−q)​(k⁡(z+1)q)​zk−q−1.g_{k}(z):=k{k(z+1)-1\choose k-1}\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\tilde{g}_{k}(z):=\sum_{q=0}^{k-1}(k-q){k(z+1)\choose q}z^{k-q-1}.

Since gk​(z)g_{k}(z) and g~k​(z)\tilde{g}_{k}(z) are polynomials in zz of order k−1k-1, it is obvious that to prove the identity (3.9, it suffices to show that

gk(r)(0)=g~k(r)(0),∀r=0,…,k−1.g_{k}^{(r)}(0)=\tilde{g}_{k}^{(r)}(0),\;\;\forall r=0,\ldots,k-1.

For example, it is easy to see that gk​(0)=g~k​(0)=kg_{k}(0)=\tilde{g}_{k}(0)=k. Let ξ:=k!\xi:=k!, while ξi1,…,im\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}} denote the product ∏i=1ki\prod_{i=1}^{k}i, where there are no numbers i1<i2<…<imi_{1}<i_{2}<\ldots<i_{m} . With this notation, we can write

gk(r)​(0)=r!​kr(k−1)!​∑1≤i1<⋯<ir≤k−1ξi1,…,ir.g_{k}^{(r)}(0)=\frac{r!k^{r}}{(k-1)!}\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-1}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r}}. (3.10)

In turn, for g~k​(z)\tilde{g}_{k}(z), we get the following:

g~k(r)​(0)=r!​∑q=0rkr−qq!​(k−q−1)!​∑q+1≤i1<⋯<ir−q≤k−1ξi1+1,…,ir−q+1.\tilde{g}_{k}^{(r)}(0)=r!\sum_{q=0}^{r}\frac{k^{r-q}}{q!(k-q-1)!}\sum_{q+1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r-q}\leq k-1}\xi_{i_{1}+1,\ldots,i_{r-q}+1}. (3.11)

Equating (3.10) to (3.11) and multiplying the resulting relation by (k−1)!/r!(k-1)!/r!, we get the equality

kr​∑1≤i1<⋯<ir≤k−1ξi1,…,ir=∑q=0r(k−1q)​kr−q​∑q+1≤i1<⋯<ir−q≤k−1ξi1+1,…,ir−q+1,k^{r}\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-1}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r}}=\sum_{q=0}^{r}{k-1\choose q}k^{r-q}\sum_{q+1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r-q}\leq k-1}\xi_{i_{1}+1,\ldots,i_{r-q}+1}, (3.12)

that remains for us to prove.

For convenience, let us denote

Dq:={ij:q+1≤i1<⋯<ir−q≤k−1}.D_{q}:=\{i_{j}:q+1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r-q}\leq k-1\}.

Obviously, the partition

D0=D0(1)​⨆D0(2)D_{0}=D^{(1)}_{0}\bigsqcup D^{(2)}_{0}

with the parts

D0(1):={ij:i1=1; 2≤i2<⋯<ir≤k−1}D^{(1)}_{0}:=\left\{i_{j}:i_{1}=1;\;2\leq i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-1\right\}

and

D0(2):={ij:2≤i1<⋯<ir≤k−1}D^{(2)}_{0}:=\left\{i_{j}:2\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-1\right\}

gives the relation

∑{ij}∈D0ξi1,…,ir\displaystyle\sum_{\{i_{j}\}\in D_{0}}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r}} =\displaystyle= ∑2≤i2<⋯<ir≤k−1ξ1,i2,…,ir+∑2≤i1<⋯<ir≤k−1ξi1,…,ir\displaystyle\sum_{2\leq i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-1}\xi_{1,i_{2},\ldots,i_{r}}+\sum_{2\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-1}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r}} (3.13)
=\displaystyle= ∑{ij}∈D1ξi1,…,ir−1+∑2≤i1<⋯<ir≤k−1ξi1,…,ir.\displaystyle\sum_{\{i_{j}\}\in D_{1}}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r-1}}+\sum_{2\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-1}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r}}.

On the other hand, making use a partition

D0=D~0(1)​⨆D~0(2)D_{0}=\tilde{D}^{(1)}_{0}\bigsqcup\tilde{D}^{(2)}_{0}

with

D~0(1):={ij:ir=k−1; 1≤i1<⋯<ir−1≤k−2}\tilde{D}^{(1)}_{0}:=\left\{i_{j}:i_{r}=k-1;\;1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r-1}\leq k-2\right\}

and

D~0(2):={ij:1≤i1<⋯<ir≤k−2},\tilde{D}^{(2)}_{0}:=\left\{i_{j}:1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-2\right\},

gives the relation

∑{ij}∈D0ξi1+1,…,ir+1\displaystyle\sum_{\{i_{j}\}\in D_{0}}\xi_{i_{1}+1,\ldots,i_{r}+1} =\displaystyle= ∑1≤i1<⋯<ir−1≤k−2ξi1+1,…,ir−1+1,k+∑1≤i1<⋯<ir≤k−2ξi1+1,…,ir+1\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r-1}\leq k-2}\xi_{i_{1}+1,\ldots,i_{r-1}+1,k}+\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-2}\xi_{i_{1}+1,\ldots,i_{r}+1} (3.14)
=\displaystyle= 1k​∑{ij}∈D1ξi1,…,ir−1+∑2≤i1<⋯<ir≤k−1ξi1,…,ir.\displaystyle\frac{1}{k}\sum_{\{i_{j}\}\in D_{1}}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r-1}}+\sum_{2\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq k-1}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r}}.

Using (3.13) and (3.14), we can rewrite (3.12) as

(k−1)​kr−1​∑{ij}∈D1ξi1,…,ir−1=∑q=1r(k−1q)​kr−q​∑{ij}∈Dqξi1+1,…,ir−q+1.(k-1)k^{r-1}\sum_{\{i_{j}\}\in D_{1}}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r-1}}=\sum_{q=1}^{r}{k-1\choose q}k^{r-q}\sum_{\{i_{j}\}\in D_{q}}\xi_{i_{1}+1,\ldots,i_{r-q}+1}.

Further, using similar partitionings of the sets D1,D2,…D_{1},D_{2},\ldots, we continue step-by-step the transformations of the initial relation. At the mm-th step we obtain this relation in the form

(k−1m)​kr−m​∑{ij}∈Dmξi1,…,ir−m=∑q=mr(k−1q)​kr−q​∑{ij}∈Dqξi1+1,…,ir−q+1.{k-1\choose m}k^{r-m}\sum_{\{i_{j}\}\in D_{m}}\xi_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r-m}}=\sum_{q=m}^{r}{k-1\choose q}k^{r-q}\sum_{\{i_{j}\}\in D_{q}}\xi_{i_{1}+1,\ldots,i_{r-q}+1}.

It is obvious that on the rr-th step we obtain a trivial identity. Thus, the lemma is proved. ∎

A direct check shows that for these examples, Fr​(2,k)=Fr​(k)F_{r}(2,k)=F_{r}(k) is true, where the polynomials Fr​(k)F_{r}(k) are the Gandhi polynomials. The examples written out above suggest that polynomials Fr​(w,k)F_{r}(w,k) should be written in the form

Fr​(w,k)=∑q≥01wq​∑j=0r−3​q−1Fr,j(q)​(w+1)r−j−3​q−1wr−j−3​q−1​kjF_{r}(w,k)=\sum_{q\geq 0}\frac{1}{w^{q}}\sum_{j=0}^{r-3q-1}F^{(q)}_{r,j}\frac{(w+1)^{r-j-3q-1}}{w^{r-j-3q-1}}k^{j}

with some coefficients Fr,j(q)F^{(q)}_{r,j}. For any fixed rr, the sum over qq is in fact finite, since, by convention, if r−3​q−1≤−1r-3q-1\leq-1, then the sum over jj is assumed to be zero.
